Why small scripts win

By Sam Writer

Small scripts are easy to read, easy to test and easy to throw away when they stop being useful. A script that does one thing well can be understood in a single sitting.

Three habits

  • Name things plainly
  • Print what you did
  • Keep a dry-run mode

Start with the smallest version that solves your problem and grow from there.

tools.name: bulk-file-renamer
tools.summary: Rename many files at once: find/replace, prefix/suffix or sequential numbering.

schema.description: Bulk rename files in a folder.

arguments.help: text to look for in file names
really rename files (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Rename many files in one folder using find/replace, a prefix or suffix, and optional sequence numbers. Stops before touching anything if two files would end up with the same name.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python bulk_file_renamer.py FOLDER [--pattern GLOB] [--find TEXT --replace TEXT]
                            [--prefix TEXT] [--suffix TEXT]
                            [--number --start N --digits N] [--apply]
```
It is a dry run by default. Add `--apply` to rename for real.
sections.Example:
```bash
python bulk_file_renamer.py ./photos --pattern "*.jpg" --find IMG --replace trip --number
```
```
IMG_0041.jpg -> trip_0041_001.jpg
IMG_0042.jpg -> trip_0042_002.jpg
Would rename 2 file(s). Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- Only files directly inside the folder are renamed, not subfolders.
- The file extension is never changed.
- Exit code 1 means a name collision was found and nothing was renamed.

tools.name: extension-counter

tools.name: line-deduper

tools.name: case-converter

tools.name: markdown-toc-generator

tools.name: bulk-find-replace

tools.name: free-space-alerter
tools.summary: Warn when free disk space drops below a size or a percentage.

schema.description: Alert when free disk space is low.

arguments.help: folders or drives to check (default: current folder)
alert below this much free space
append each result to this file

sections.Purpose: Warn before a disk fills up. Checks one or more folders or drives against a minimum amount (or percentage) of free space and exits with 1 if any is too low, so a scheduler or script can react.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python free_space_alerter.py [PATH ...] [--min-free SIZE] [--min-percent N] [--log FILE]
```
`--min-free` takes units like `500MB` or `20GB` (default `10GB`). `--log` appends a timestamped line for every check.
sections.Example:
```bash
python free_space_alerter.py C:/ D:/ --min-free 50GB --log space.log
```
```
LOW  C:/  42.3 GB free (9%)
OK   D:/  721.1 GB free (77%)
```
sections.Notes:
- Exit code 0 means every disk is fine, 1 means at least one is low or unreadable.
- Pair it with cron or Windows Task Scheduler for a daily check.
- Read-only apart from the optional log file.

tools.name: folder-size-history
tools.summary: Record a folder's size over time in a CSV and show how it has changed.

schema.description: Track a folder's size over time.

arguments.help: CSV file to append to (default: folder_sizes.csv)
show the history instead of recording a new entry

sections.Purpose: Keep a running record of how big a folder is, so you can see what grows over time: downloads, caches, project builds. Each run adds one line to a CSV.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python folder_size_history.py FOLDER [--log FILE.csv] [--show]
```
Without `--show` it records the current size and then prints the history for that folder. With `--show` it only prints the history. Run it from a scheduler to build up a timeline.
sections.Example:
```bash
python folder_size_history.py ~/Downloads --log sizes.csv
```
```
Recorded 3.4 GB in 812 file(s) at 2026-10-31 09:00:12.
2026-10-30 09:00:05      3.1 GB     790 files
2026-10-31 09:00:12      3.4 GB     812 files  (310.2 MB change)
```
sections.Notes:
- The CSV has the columns `timestamp, folder, bytes, files`, so it opens in any spreadsheet.
- One log file can track several folders; the history shows one folder at a time.
- It only appends to the log you name and never touches the folder being measured.

tools.name: hosts-file-viewer
tools.summary: Show the entries of the hosts file as a readable table.

schema.description: Show the hosts file as a table.

arguments.help: only show entries containing this text

sections.Purpose: Read the hosts file without squinting at raw text. Shows each entry's address, names and note, hides disabled lines unless you ask, and warns when the same name points at two different addresses.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python hosts_file_viewer.py [--file PATH] [--search TEXT] [--all]
```
By default it reads `/etc/hosts`, or `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows.
sections.Example:
```bash
python hosts_file_viewer.py --search nas
```
```
line  address           names                                   note
   6  192.168.1.5       nas.local, nas
   8  10.0.0.1          nas.local
2 entries from /etc/hosts.
Warning: names pointing to different addresses: nas.local
```
sections.Notes:
- Read-only. Editing the hosts file needs administrator rights and is not done here.
- Lines starting with `#` are treated as disabled entries only when they look like `IP name`.

tools.name: csv-cleaner
tools.summary: Tidy a CSV file: trim cells, drop blank rows and normalize the header names.

arguments.help: really write the file (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Fix the usual CSV annoyances in one pass: stray spaces around values, completely blank rows, short rows, and headers like `  First Name! ` that are awkward to work with.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python csv_cleaner.py FILE [-o OUTPUT] [--keep-headers] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it prints what it would change. Pass `--apply` to write the result to `-o`, or over the input file if you give no `-o`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python csv_cleaner.py contacts.csv -o contacts_clean.csv --apply
```
```
5 row(s) in, 3 out: 2 blank removed, 4 cell(s) trimmed, 1 short row(s) padded.
Header: first_name,last_name,age
Wrote contacts_clean.csv.
```
sections.Notes:
- The delimiter (comma, semicolon, tab or pipe) is detected and kept.
- Headers become lowercase `snake_case`; repeated names get `_2`, `_3`.
- Use `-o` while you're unsure, so the original file stays untouched.

tools.name: csv-column-stats
tools.summary: Summarize every column of a CSV: counts, blanks, min/max/mean or top values.

schema.description: Per-column statistics for a CSV file.

sections.Purpose: Get a fast overview of a CSV file before you work with it. For each column you see how many values are filled or blank and how many are unique, plus min, max, mean and median for numbers or the most common values for text.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python csv_column_stats.py FILE [--delimiter CHAR]
```
sections.Example:
```bash
python csv_column_stats.py sales.csv
```
```
120 data row(s), 3 column(s)

region  [text]  filled=120 blank=0 unique=4
    top: north (41), south (38), east (27)
amount  [number]  filled=118 blank=2 unique=97
    min=4.5 max=980 mean=212.33 median=180
```
sections.Notes:
- A column counts as numeric only if every filled value is a number (thousands commas are fine).
- Read-only.

tools.name: json-pretty-printer
tools.summary: Format, minify or validate JSON, with clear error positions.

arguments.help: write the result to this file

sections.Purpose: Make JSON readable, shrink it, or just find out whether it is valid. When parsing fails it shows the offending line with a pointer to the exact column.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python json_pretty_printer.py [FILE] [--indent N] [--sort-keys] [--minify] [--check]
                              [-o OUTPUT --apply]
```
With no file it reads standard input. Output goes to the terminal; writing a file needs both `-o` and `--apply`.
sections.Example:
```bash
echo '{"b": 1, "a": [1, 2]}' | python json_pretty_printer.py --sort-keys
```
```
{
  "a": [
    1,
    2
  ],
  "b": 1
}
```
sections.Notes:
- Exit code 1 means the JSON was invalid, which is handy in scripts and pre-commit hooks.
- Non-ASCII characters are kept as they are, not escaped.

tools.name: json-yaml-converter
tools.summary: Convert between JSON and YAML files.

schema.description: Convert JSON to YAML or YAML to JSON.

arguments.help: target format (default: the opposite of the input)
write the result to this file
really write --output (default only prints the result)

sections.Purpose: Convert configuration and data files between JSON and YAML, keeping key order and non-ASCII text intact.
sections.Install:
Needs PyYAML:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python json_yaml_converter.py FILE [--to json|yaml] [-o OUTPUT --apply]
```
The input format comes from the file extension (`.yaml` / `.yml` or anything else as JSON), and the target defaults to the opposite one. The result is printed unless you pass `-o` together with `--apply`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python json_yaml_converter.py config.json
```
```
name: demo
ports:
- 80
- 443
debug: false
```
sections.Notes:
- Uses `yaml.safe_load`, so YAML files cannot run code.
- YAML features with no JSON equivalent (anchors, comments) are resolved or dropped in the conversion.
- Invalid input exits with 1 and an error message.

tools.name: csv-to-json
tools.summary: Convert a CSV file into JSON records (or JSON Lines).

arguments.help: detect numbers, booleans and empty values
write the result to this file
really write --output (default only prints the result)

sections.Purpose: Turn a CSV file into JSON that code or APIs can use: a list of objects keyed by the header names, or JSON Lines with one object per line.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python csv_to_json.py FILE [--types] [--lines] [--delimiter CHAR] [-o OUTPUT --apply]
```
Everything stays text unless you pass `--types`, which converts numbers and `true`/`false` and turns empty cells into `null`. The result is printed unless you pass `-o` with `--apply`.
sections.Notes:
- Short rows are padded with empty values; extra cells beyond the header are dropped.
- A UTF-8 byte-order mark at the start of the file is handled.

tools.name: json-to-csv
tools.summary: Flatten JSON records into a CSV file.

arguments.help: path to the list inside the JSON, e.g. data.items
write the CSV to this file
really write --output (default only prints the CSV)

sections.Purpose: Open JSON data in a spreadsheet. Takes a list of JSON objects (for example an API response) and writes one CSV row per object, flattening nested objects into dotted column names.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python json_to_csv.py FILE [--key PATH] [-o OUTPUT --apply]
```
If the file is an object holding one list of records (like `{"items": [...]}`) it is found automatically. Otherwise give the list's path with `--key`, for example `--key data.items`. The CSV is printed unless you pass `-o` with `--apply`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python json_to_csv.py users.json
```
```
id,name,address.city
1,Ada,London
2,Lin,Shanghai
```
sections.Notes:
- Columns are the union of every key, in the order they first appear; missing values are blank.
- Lists inside a record are written as JSON text in a single cell.
- Anything that isn't a list of objects stops with an error and exit code 1.

tools.name: csv-merger
tools.summary: Merge several CSV files into one, matching columns by name.

schema.description: Merge CSV files with matching columns.

arguments.help: add a 'source' column with each row's file name
really write the output (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Combine several CSV files (monthly exports, per-region sheets) into a single file. Columns are matched by name, so files don't need identical column order, and missing values are left blank.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python csv_merger.py FILE FILE [FILE ...] [-o OUTPUT] [--add-source] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it reports what the merged file would contain. Pass `--apply` to write it (default output `merged.csv`). `--add-source` adds a `source` column with each row's file name.
sections.Example:
```bash
python csv_merger.py jan.csv feb.csv mar.csv -o q1.csv --add-source --apply
```
```
jan.csv: 120 row(s), 4 column(s)
feb.csv: 98 row(s), 4 column(s)
mar.csv: 131 row(s), 5 column(s)
Merged: 349 row(s), 6 column(s): date, region, amount, notes, channel, source
Wrote q1.csv.
```
sections.Notes:
- The input files are never modified.
- All files must use the same delimiter (set it with `--delimiter`).

tools.name: csv-splitter
tools.summary: Split a big CSV file into smaller parts, repeating the header in each.

schema.description: Split a CSV file into parts.

arguments.help: really write the parts (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Break a huge CSV into smaller files that open in a spreadsheet or fit an upload limit. Every part gets the original header row.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python csv_splitter.py FILE [--rows N] [-o OUTDIR] [--delimiter CHAR] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it lists the parts it would create. Pass `--apply` to write them.
sections.Example:
```bash
python csv_splitter.py orders.csv --rows 50000 -o parts --apply
```
```
parts/orders_part001.csv  (50000 rows)
parts/orders_part002.csv  (50000 rows)
parts/orders_part003.csv  (12874 rows)
Wrote 3 part(s).
```
sections.Notes:
- The file is streamed, so memory use stays small however large it is.
- The original file is never changed.
- Parts are named `<name>_part001.csv`, `<name>_part002.csv` and so on.

tools.name: csv-deduper
tools.summary: Remove duplicate rows from a CSV, comparing all columns or just the ones you pick.

schema.description: Remove duplicate rows from a CSV file.

arguments.help: comma-separated columns that define a duplicate
really write the file (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Remove repeated rows from a CSV. By default a row is a duplicate only if every column matches; with `--columns` you choose which columns define a duplicate, for example just `email`.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python csv_deduper.py FILE [--columns a,b] [--keep first|last] [-i] [-o OUTPUT] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it reports how many duplicates it found. Pass `--apply` to write the result, to `-o` or over the input.
sections.Example:
```bash
python csv_deduper.py contacts.csv --columns email -i -o unique.csv --apply
```
```
2400 data row(s), 187 duplicate(s), 2213 kept.
Wrote unique.csv.
```
sections.Notes:
- Surrounding spaces are ignored when comparing values.
- `--keep last` keeps the most recent occurrence, which suits exports sorted oldest first.
- Row order is preserved.

tools.name: excel-to-csv
tools.summary: Export the sheets of an Excel workbook (.xlsx) to CSV files.

arguments.help: really write the CSV files (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Turn an Excel workbook into plain CSV files, one per sheet, so the data can go into scripts, databases or version control.
sections.Install:
Needs openpyxl:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python excel_to_csv.py FILE.xlsx [--sheet NAME] [-o OUTDIR] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it lists the files it would create. Pass `--apply` to write them. Files are named `<workbook>_<sheet>.csv`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python excel_to_csv.py budget.xlsx -o csv --apply
```
```
Income: 14 row(s) -> csv/budget_Income.csv
Expenses: 52 row(s) -> csv/budget_Expenses.csv
Wrote 2 file(s).
```
sections.Notes:
- Formulas are exported as their last calculated values (as Excel saved them).
- Dates become ISO text (`2026-01-05`, with the time only when there is one) and whole numbers lose the trailing `.0`.
- Only the modern `.xlsx` format is supported, not the old `.xls`.

tools.name: password-strength-checker
tools.summary: Score a password and explain what makes it weak. The password is never echoed.

schema.description: Check how strong a password is.

arguments.help: password to check (default: prompt or stdin)

sections.Purpose: Find out whether a password is any good and why. It estimates strength from length and character variety, and flags common passwords, repeated characters and easy sequences like `1234` or `qwer`. The password itself is never printed back.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python password_strength_checker.py [PASSWORD]
```
Without an argument it asks for the password with hidden input (or reads one line from a pipe). Typing a real password as an argument can leave it in your shell history, so prefer the prompt for anything you actually use. The exit code is 0 for strong passwords (3/4 or better) and 1 otherwise.
sections.Example:
```bash
python password_strength_checker.py "summer2024"
```
```
Strength: very weak (0/4), about 33 bits
Length:   10 characters
- It is short (10 characters; aim for 12 or more).
- It mixes too few kinds of characters (use upper, lower, digits, symbols).
```
sections.Notes:
- The bit estimate is a rough upper bound and ignores dictionary attacks, so treat it as a guide, not a guarantee.
- Longer passphrases beat short, complicated ones.
- Nothing is stored or sent anywhere; everything runs locally.

tools.name: password-generator
tools.summary: Generate strong random passwords and passphrases using the secrets module.

arguments.help: avoid look-alike characters such as O, 0, l and 1
make a passphrase of this many words instead

sections.Purpose: Create strong random passwords or easy-to-type passphrases. It uses Python's `secrets` module, which draws from the operating system's secure random source, not the ordinary `random` module.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python password_generator.py [-n COUNT] [-l LENGTH] [--no-symbols] [--no-ambiguous]
python password_generator.py --passphrase WORDS [--separator CHAR] [-n COUNT]
```
Passwords always contain a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter, a digit and (unless turned off) a symbol.
sections.Example:
```bash
python password_generator.py -n 2 -l 18
python password_generator.py --passphrase 4
```
```
r7#Kd!mQ2vZ_e8Wb+L
Xp4%tN9hC&uA3sEk@Y
Maple-Cafe-Wolf-Jade
```
sections.Notes:
- Output goes to the terminal only; nothing is saved or sent anywhere.
- The built-in word list is small (181 words, roughly 7.5 bits per word), so use 6 or more words for passphrases that matter.
- `--no-ambiguous` skips characters that look alike, such as `O`, `0`, `l` and `1`.

tools.name: hash-checker
tools.summary: Check that a file matches an expected checksum (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 or SHA-512).

schema.description: Verify a file against an expected checksum.

arguments.help: expected hash, or a path to a checksum file
hash algorithm (default: guessed from the hash length)

sections.Purpose: Confirm that a download is exactly what the publisher intended. Give it the file and the checksum from the website, and it tells you whether they match.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python hash_checker.py FILE EXPECTED [-a md5|sha1|sha256|sha512]
```
`EXPECTED` can be the hash itself, text like `sha256:<hash>`, or the path of a checksum file such as `ubuntu.iso.sha256`. The algorithm is guessed from the hash length unless you pass `-a`. The exit code is 0 on a match and 1 on a mismatch.
sections.Example:
```bash
python hash_checker.py installer.iso 9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08
```
```
OK: installer.iso matches the expected sha256 hash.
```
sections.Notes:
- Prefer SHA-256 or SHA-512. MD5 and SHA-1 only guard against accidents, not tampering.
- The comparison uses a constant-time check and ignores letter case.
- Read-only.

tools.name: file-hasher
tools.summary: Print MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 (and more) hashes for files in one read.

schema.description: Hash files with one or more algorithms.

arguments.help: print in sha256sum style ('hash  file') for a single algorithm

sections.Purpose: Compute checksums for one file or a whole folder. Several algorithms are calculated in a single pass over each file, so hashing a big file with MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 costs one read.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python file_hasher.py PATH [PATH ...] [-a md5|sha1|sha256|sha512] [-r] [--sums]
```
Use `-a` more than once for several algorithms (default `sha256`). `--sums` prints `hash  file` lines like the `sha256sum` tool, which you can keep as a checksum list.
sections.Example:
```bash
python file_hasher.py setup.zip -a md5 -a sha256
```
```
setup.zip
  md5    5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592
  sha256 2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824
```
sections.Notes:
- Folders are listed non-recursively unless you pass `-r`.
- Unreadable files are reported on stderr and the exit code becomes 1.
- Pair it with `hash-checker` to verify downloads.

tools.name: checksum-manifest
tools.summary: Write a checksum list for a folder, then verify the folder against it later.

schema.description: Create or verify a folder checksum manifest.

arguments.help: check the folder against the manifest instead of creating one
really write the manifest (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Prove that a folder hasn't changed. Create a list of SHA-256 checksums for every file, then verify the folder against that list later to see which files changed, went missing or were added. Good for backups, releases and archives.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python checksum_manifest.py FOLDER [--manifest FILE] [--apply]      # create
python checksum_manifest.py FOLDER [--manifest FILE] --verify       # check
```
Creating is a dry run by default; pass `--apply` to write the manifest (default `SHA256SUMS.txt` inside the folder). Verifying is read-only and exits 1 if anything changed or is missing.
sections.Example:
```bash
python checksum_manifest.py ./release --apply
python checksum_manifest.py ./release --verify
```
```
CHANGED front/app.js
NEW     notes.txt
48 file(s) checked: 1 changed, 0 missing, 1 new.
```
sections.Notes:
- The manifest uses the `sha256sum` layout (`hash  path`), so standard tools can verify it too.
- The manifest file itself is never listed in its own checksums.
- New files are reported but don't count as a failure.

tools.name: secret-scanner
tools.summary: Scan a folder for accidentally committed secrets such as API keys and private keys.

sections.Purpose: Catch credentials before they leak. Scans every text file in a folder for AWS keys, GitHub and Slack tokens, Google and Stripe keys, private key blocks and hard-coded `password = "..."` style assignments.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python secret_scanner.py [FOLDER]
```
The exit code is 1 when something is found, so it works as a pre-commit or CI check.
sections.Example:
```bash
python secret_scanner.py ./my-project
```
```
my-project/config.py:12  AWS access key  AKI**********XYZ
my-project/deploy.sh:4  Hard-coded credential  pas**********ue"
2 possible secret(s) found.
```
sections.Notes:
- Matches are masked in the output, so the report itself doesn't leak anything.
- Lines containing placeholders such as `your_key`, `example` or `${...}` are ignored.
- `.git`, `node_modules`, virtual environments, binary files and files over 2 MB are skipped.
- It is a quick pattern check, not a full audit. If a real secret turns up, rotate it: deleting it from the file doesn't remove it from history.

tools.name: env-file-auditor
tools.summary: Audit a .env file for empty, duplicate, weak or missing values. Values are never printed.

arguments.help: .gitignore to check the file is excluded

sections.Purpose: Check a `.env` file before it causes trouble: empty values, leftover placeholders, weak secrets, duplicate names, variables that exist in `.env.example` but are missing, and whether the file is excluded by `.gitignore`. It only talks about names and line numbers, so values never appear in the output.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python env_file_auditor.py FILE [--example .env.example] [--gitignore .gitignore]
```
The exit code is 1 when any problem is found.
sections.Example:
```bash
python env_file_auditor.py .env --example .env.example --gitignore .gitignore
```
```
line 2   DB_PASSWORD  looks like a weak secret
line 5   STRIPE_KEY  is empty
file     SMTP_HOST  is in the example file but missing here
12 variable(s) checked, 3 problem(s).
```
sections.Notes:
- A secret counts as weak if its name contains KEY, TOKEN, SECRET or PASSWORD and the value is shorter than 8 characters or a common word.
- `export NAME=value` lines and quoted values are understood.
- Read-only. Never commit your real `.env` file; commit a `.env.example` with placeholder values instead.

tools.name: token-generator
tools.summary: Create random tokens: URL-safe, hex, Base32, numeric PINs or UUIDs.

arguments.help: bytes of randomness (digits for numeric; ignored for uuid)
text to put in front, e.g. sk_

sections.Purpose: Make random tokens for API keys, session secrets, invite codes, one-time PINs or unique IDs. All randomness comes from Python's `secrets` module, which is meant for security use.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python token_generator.py [--kind urlsafe|hex|base32|numeric|uuid] [-b BYTES] [-p PREFIX] [-n COUNT]
```
`--bytes` sets how much randomness goes in (32 bytes is 256 bits). For `numeric` it is the number of digits.
sections.Example:
```bash
python token_generator.py --kind hex -b 16 -p sk_ -n 2
```
```
sk_9c1e4f0b7a3d28e5b6f1a0c4d7e92b83
sk_41d8a6e0c9f3b27d5e8a1c4f60b93d27
```
sections.Notes:
- A prefix such as `sk_` or `pk_` makes keys easy to recognise and easy to find with `secret-scanner`.
- Numeric PINs are short by nature; use them only where attempts are rate-limited.
- Tokens are printed and not stored. Save them in a password manager or environment variable straight away.

tools.name: base64-tool
tools.summary: Encode or decode text and files as Base64 (standard or URL-safe).

schema.description: Base64 encode or decode text and files.

arguments.help: read the input from this file
write the result to this file
really write --output (default only prints text results)

sections.Purpose: Encode or decode Base64, for example to inspect a token, embed a small file in a config, or turn a binary file into text and back. Supports both the standard and the URL-safe alphabets.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python base64_tool.py [TEXT] [-f FILE] [-d] [--url-safe] [-o OUTPUT --apply]
```
Input comes from the text argument, `--file`, or standard input. Add `-d` to decode. Text results are printed; binary results need `-o FILE --apply` so they aren't dumped into your terminal.
sections.Example:
```bash
python base64_tool.py "hello world"
python base64_tool.py -d aGVsbG8gd29ybGQ=
```
```
aGVsbG8gd29ybGQ=
hello world
```
sections.Notes:
- Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. Anyone can decode it, so never use it to hide secrets.
- Decoding ignores whitespace and accepts input without `=` padding.
- Invalid input exits with code 1 and a message.

tools.name: permission-auditor
tools.summary: Find risky file permissions on Linux and macOS, and optionally tighten them.

schema.description: Audit file permissions under a folder.

arguments.help: really tighten the permissions (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Spot permission mistakes that quietly open up your files on Linux and macOS: files anyone can write, shared folders missing the sticky bit, setuid/setgid programs, and private keys (SSH keys, `.pem`, `.key`) that other users can read.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python permission_auditor.py [FOLDER] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it lists each issue with the current and the safer mode. Pass `--apply` to change the permissions. On Windows, which has no Unix permission bits, it explains that and exits cleanly.
sections.Example:
```bash
python permission_auditor.py ~/.ssh
```
```
0644 -> 0600  private key readable by others: /home/me/.ssh/id_ed25519
Would fix 1 issue(s).
Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- Fixes only remove the risky bit (for example `o-w`) or restrict keys to the owner; they never add permissions.
- Symlinks are not followed, and `.git` and `node_modules` are skipped.
- Always review the dry-run list first. Some programs, such as `sudo`, are meant to be setuid.

tools.name: image-resizer
tools.summary: Resize images by width, height or percentage, keeping the aspect ratio.

schema.description: Resize images, keeping the aspect ratio.

arguments.help: scale by this percentage (50 = half size)
really write the images (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Shrink or enlarge photos and screenshots while keeping their proportions: by width, by height, to fit inside a box, or by a percentage.
sections.Install:
Needs Pillow:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python image_resizer.py PATH [PATH ...] [--width PX] [--height PX] [--percent N]
                        [-o OUTDIR] [--apply]
```
`PATH` can be image files or folders. Give both `--width` and `--height` to fit the image inside that box. Dry run by default: it lists the new sizes. Pass `--apply` to write the resized copies to `OUTDIR` (default `resized`). Originals are never touched.
sections.Example:
```bash
python image_resizer.py ./photos --width 800 -o small --apply
```
```
beach.jpg: 4032x3024 -> 800x600
sunset.jpg: 3000x2000 -> 800x533
Resized 2 image(s).
```
sections.Notes:
- Supports PNG, JPG, WEBP, GIF (first frame only), BMP and TIFF.
- Files that aren't readable images are skipped with a message.
- Resizing uses the high-quality Lanczos filter; JPEG output is saved at quality 90.

tools.name: image-converter
tools.summary: Convert images between PNG, JPG, WEBP, GIF, BMP and TIFF.

arguments.help: really write the images (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Change images from one format to another, for example PNG screenshots to smaller JPGs, or JPGs to modern WEBP. Transparent PNGs are flattened onto white when saved as JPG, since JPG can't store transparency.
sections.Install:
Needs Pillow:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python image_converter.py PATH [PATH ...] --to png|jpg|webp|gif|bmp|tiff
                          [--quality N] [-o OUTDIR] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it lists what would be converted. Pass `--apply` to write the new files into `OUTDIR` (default `converted`). The originals are kept.
sections.Example:
```bash
python image_converter.py ./shots --to webp --quality 80 --apply
```
```
login.png -> login.webp
home.png -> home.webp
Converted 2 image(s).
```
sections.Notes:
- Files already in the target format are skipped.
- `--quality` applies to JPG and WEBP.
- Animated GIFs convert to their first frame in other formats.

tools.name: image-metadata-reader
tools.summary: Show size, format and EXIF details (camera, date, location flag) for images.

sections.Purpose: See what is hidden inside an image file: dimensions, format, colour mode, resolution and, for photos, the EXIF details such as camera, capture date and orientation. It also warns when a photo carries GPS location data, which you may want to remove before sharing.
sections.Install:
Needs Pillow:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python image_metadata_reader.py PATH [PATH ...] [--json]
```
`PATH` can be image files or folders.
sections.Example:
```bash
python image_metadata_reader.py holiday.jpg
```
```
holiday.jpg  JPEG 4032x3024 (12.19 MP, RGB, 2481023 bytes, 1 frame(s))
    Make: Apple
    Model: iPhone 15
    DateTimeOriginal: 2026:07:14 18:22:09
    location data: PRESENT (GPS tags found)
1 image(s).
```
sections.Notes:
- Read-only.
- The exit code is 1 if any file couldn't be read as an image.
- To strip location data from photos, see the `exif-stripper` tool planned later in this challenge.

tools.name: screenshot-organizer
tools.summary: File screenshots into year/month folders, using the date in the file name when there is one.

arguments.help: regex for file names that count as screenshots
really move the files (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Clear a desktop or downloads folder full of screenshots by filing them into `YEAR/YEAR-MONTH` folders. The date comes from the file name when it contains one (as macOS, Windows and Android screenshots do), and from the modified time otherwise.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python screenshot_organizer.py [FOLDER] [--pattern REGEX] [--layout year-month|month] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default; pass `--apply` to move the files. A file counts as a screenshot when it is an image whose name matches `--pattern` (default: screenshot, screen shot, snip or capture).
sections.Example:
```bash
python screenshot_organizer.py ~/Desktop
```
```
Screenshot 2026-03-01 at 09.30.15.png -> 2026/2026-03/
Screenshot 2026-03-02 at 14.05.00.png -> 2026/2026-03/
Would move 2 screenshot(s). Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- Only files directly inside the folder are moved; other images are left alone.
- A file is skipped if the destination already has one with the same name.
- Recognised date formats: `2026-03-01`, `2026_03_01`, `2026.03.01` and `20260301`.

tools.name: thumbnail-generator
tools.summary: Make thumbnails for every image in a folder.

schema.description: Create thumbnails for a folder of images.

arguments.help: really write the thumbnails (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Create small preview versions of every image in a folder, for galleries, websites or quick browsing. Photos taken in portrait mode are turned the right way up first.
sections.Install:
Needs Pillow:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python thumbnail_generator.py FOLDER [--size PX] [--square] [--suffix TEXT] [-o OUTDIR] [--apply]
```
`--size` is the longest side (default 200). `--square` crops each thumbnail to an exact square. Dry run by default; pass `--apply` to write the files into `FOLDER/thumbs` (or `-o`).
sections.Example:
```bash
python thumbnail_generator.py ./photos --size 160 --square --apply
```
```
beach_01.jpg -> beach_01_thumb.jpg (160x160)
sunset.jpg -> sunset_thumb.jpg (160x160)
Created 2 thumbnail(s) in photos/thumbs.
```
sections.Notes:
- Without `--square` the aspect ratio is kept and small images are never enlarged.
- Unreadable files are skipped with a message.
- Originals are never changed.

tools.name: image-rotator
tools.summary: Rotate, flip or straighten images in bulk.

schema.description: Rotate or flip images in bulk.

arguments.help: rotate clockwise by this many degrees
turn photos upright using their EXIF orientation flag
really write the images (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Fix sideways photos or mirror a batch of images. Rotate clockwise by 90, 180 or 270 degrees, flip horizontally or vertically, or turn photos upright using the orientation flag the camera stored.
sections.Install:
Needs Pillow:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python image_rotator.py PATH [PATH ...] [--rotate 90|180|270] [--flip horizontal|vertical]
                        [--fix-orientation] [-o OUTDIR] [--apply]
```
At least one of the three actions is required, and they can be combined. Dry run by default; pass `--apply` to write the results into `OUTDIR` (default `rotated`).
sections.Example:
```bash
python image_rotator.py ./scans --rotate 90 --apply
```
```
page1.png: 2480x3508 -> 3508x2480
page2.png: 2480x3508 -> 3508x2480
Saved 2 image(s).
```
sections.Notes:
- Rotation is clockwise.
- Originals are never overwritten; results go to the output folder.
- Pixel quality is preserved for 90 degree turns and flips (no resampling).

tools.name: qr-generator
tools.summary: Generate QR codes from text or URLs: print them in the terminal or save SVG/PNG files.

arguments.help: error correction: L 7%%, M 15%%, Q 25%%, H 30%% (default M)
really write --output (default only prints the code)

sections.Purpose: Turn a web address, Wi-Fi details or any short text into a QR code. It draws the code right in the terminal and can also save it as an SVG (sharp at any size) or PNG file.
sections.Install:
Needs the `qrcode` package (PNG output also uses Pillow):
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python qr_generator.py TEXT [--level L|M|Q|H] [--ascii] [-o FILE.svg|FILE.png --apply]
```
The code is always printed. To save a file, pass `-o` together with `--apply`; the extension picks the format. Higher error-correction levels survive more damage but make the code denser.
sections.Example:
```bash
python qr_generator.py "https://example.com" --ascii
```
```
QR version 2, 29 modules wide, level M.
```
(The code itself is drawn above that line.)
sections.Notes:
- Scan the result with a phone before printing or sharing it.
- `--ascii` uses `##` characters, which works in any terminal; the default block characters are more compact.
- SVG output needs no image library; PNG output needs Pillow.

tools.name: grayscale-converter
tools.summary: Convert a folder of images to grayscale (black and white).

arguments.help: really write the images (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Turn colour images into black and white in bulk, for printing, document scans or a consistent look. Transparent areas stay transparent, and an optional contrast stretch makes flat-looking scans pop.
sections.Install:
Needs Pillow:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python grayscale_converter.py PATH [PATH ...] [--contrast] [-o OUTDIR] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it lists what would be converted. Pass `--apply` to write the results into `OUTDIR` (default `grayscale`). Originals are never changed.
sections.Example:
```bash
python grayscale_converter.py ./scans --contrast --apply
```
```
page1.png -> grayscale/page1.png (L)
logo.png -> grayscale/logo.png (LA)
Converted 2 image(s).
```
sections.Notes:
- `L` means plain grayscale; `LA` means grayscale with an alpha (transparency) channel.
- Unreadable files are skipped with a message.
- Uses the standard luminance formula, so greens look brighter than blues, as the eye sees them.

tools.name: photo-date-renamer
tools.summary: Rename photos using the date and time they were taken (EXIF), falling back to the file date.

schema.description: Rename photos by their capture date.

arguments.help: strftime pattern for the new name (default %%Y-%%m-%%d_%%H%%M%%S)
really rename the files (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Give photos meaningful, sortable names such as `2026-01-05_101500.jpg` based on when they were actually taken. The time comes from the photo's EXIF data; if a file has none, its modified date is used instead.
sections.Install:
Needs Pillow:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python photo_date_renamer.py FOLDER [--format PATTERN] [--apply]
```
`--format` is a [strftime](https://strftime.org) pattern (default `%Y-%m-%d_%H%M%S`). Dry run by default; pass `--apply` to rename. Photos taken in the same second get `-2`, `-3` added.
sections.Example:
```bash
python photo_date_renamer.py ./camera-roll
```
```
IMG_4021.JPG -> 2026-07-14_182209.jpg  (EXIF)
WhatsApp Image.jpeg -> 2026-07-15_090511.jpeg  (file date)
Would rename 2 photo(s). Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- Extensions are lowercased. Files that already have the target name are left alone.
- A rename is skipped if a file with the new name already exists.
- Messaging apps often strip EXIF data, so those photos fall back to the file date.

tools.name: gif-frame-extractor
tools.summary: Save every frame of an animated GIF as a separate image.

schema.description: Extract the frames of an animated GIF.

arguments.help: really write the frames (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Split an animated GIF into its individual frames, for editing, sprite sheets or just looking at one moment. It also tells you how many frames there are and how long each one lasts.
sections.Install:
Needs Pillow:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python gif_frame_extractor.py FILE.gif [--format png|jpg|webp] [-o OUTDIR] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it lists the frames it would write. Pass `--apply` to write them into `OUTDIR` (default `<name>_frames` next to the GIF).
sections.Example:
```bash
python gif_frame_extractor.py loading.gif --apply
```
```
loading.gif: 4 frame(s), 480 ms in total
  loading_frame001.png  (120 ms)
  loading_frame002.png  (120 ms)
  loading_frame003.png  (120 ms)
  loading_frame004.png  (120 ms)
Wrote 4 frame(s) to loading_frames.
```
sections.Notes:
- A still (non-animated) image counts as one frame.
- `jpg` output has no transparency; PNG and WEBP keep it.
- The GIF itself is never modified.

tools.name: habit-tracker
tools.summary: Track daily habits and streaks from the terminal. Data lives in a small JSON file.

arguments.help: check/uncheck a habit for a day, list habits, or show a report
pretend today is this date (handy for testing)

sections.Purpose: Keep a streak going. Check off habits each day from the terminal and see your current streak, best streak and a two-week history for each one.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python habit_tracker.py check NAME [--date YYYY-MM-DD] [--file FILE]
python habit_tracker.py uncheck NAME [--date YYYY-MM-DD]
python habit_tracker.py list
python habit_tracker.py report [--today YYYY-MM-DD]
```
Data is kept in a small JSON file (default `~/.habits.json`; choose another with `--file`). This file is the tool's own storage, so `check` writes to it straight away.
sections.Example:
```bash
python habit_tracker.py report --file habits.json --today 2026-01-07
```
```

```
sections.Notes:
- A streak survives until the end of today, so checking in yesterday but not yet today still counts.
- `--today` lets you test or backfill without changing your clock.
- Checking the same day twice does nothing extra.

tools.name: pomodoro-timer
tools.summary: Run focus and break cycles with a terminal countdown (the Pomodoro technique).

arguments.help: read the numbers as minutes or seconds (seconds suits a demo)
only print the schedule, don't wait
clock time the plan starts at (09:00)
no sound at the end of a phase

sections.Purpose: Work in focused bursts with a countdown in your terminal: 25 minutes of focus, a short break, and a longer break after four sessions. Every phase ends with a terminal bell.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python pomodoro_timer.py [--focus MIN] [--break MIN] [--long-break MIN] [--sessions N]
                         [--rounds N] [--unit minutes|seconds] [--plan] [--start HH:MM] [--no-bell]
```
Run it with no options for the classic 25/5/15 cycle. `--plan` prints the schedule with clock times and exits, which is useful for planning your day. `--unit seconds` shrinks every duration to seconds for a quick demo. Press Ctrl+C to stop.
sections.Example:
```bash
python pomodoro_timer.py --plan --start 09:00
```
```
09:00  Focus 1/4    25 min
09:25  Short break  5 min
09:30  Focus 2/4    25 min
09:55  Short break  5 min
10:00  Focus 3/4    25 min
10:25  Short break  5 min
10:30  Focus 4/4    25 min
10:55  Long break   15 min
Ends at 11:10. 100 minutes of focus in 8 phases.
```
sections.Notes:
- The countdown updates in place on one line and needs a real terminal; on the website use `--plan`.
- The final focus session of a round is followed by the long break.
- Use `--no-bell` if the sound is unwelcome.

tools.name: todo-cli
tools.summary: A simple add / list / done / remove task manager. Tasks live in a small JSON file.

arguments.help: task text (add) or task numbers (done, undo, remove)

sections.Purpose: A tiny task list for the terminal: add tasks with a priority, see what is open, tick things off. High-priority tasks float to the top.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python todo_cli.py add TEXT... [-p high|normal|low]
python todo_cli.py list [--all]
python todo_cli.py done NUMBER...      # also: undo, remove
python todo_cli.py clear-done
```
Tasks are stored in a small JSON file (default `~/.todos.json`, change it with `--file`). That file is the tool's own storage, so changes are saved straight away.
sections.Example:
```bash
python todo_cli.py list --file todos.json
```
```
[ ]   1 ! Write the weekly report
[ ]   4 ! Renew passport
[ ]   2   Book dentist appointment
[x]   3   Reply to Sam
3 open, 1 done.
```
sections.Notes:
- `!` marks open high-priority tasks. Task numbers never get reused.
- `list` hides finished tasks unless you pass `--all`.
- An unknown task number stops with an error and exit code 1.

tools.name: journal-cli
tools.summary: Append dated, timestamped entries to a markdown journal, and read them back.

arguments.help: text to add (omit to read instead)
day for the entry, YYYY-MM-DD (default: today)
time for the entry, HH:MM (default: now)
show the last N days of entries

sections.Purpose: Capture a thought in a few seconds. Each entry is added to a plain markdown file, grouped under a heading for the day and stamped with the time, so your journal stays readable in any editor and works with Obsidian, Notion imports or git.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python journal_cli.py TEXT... [--date YYYY-MM-DD] [--time HH:MM] [--file FILE]   # add an entry
python journal_cli.py --show DAYS [--file FILE]                                     # read recent days
python journal_cli.py --search WORD [--file FILE]                                   # find entries
```
The default file is `~/journal.md`. Without text it shows the last three days. This file is the tool's own storage, so entries are saved straight away.
sections.Example:
```bash
python journal_cli.py --show 2 --file journal.md
```
```
2026-01-05
- 09:10 Started the day with a long walk.
- 18:45 Finished the draft and sent it out.
2026-01-06
- 08:30 Planned the week.
- 21:00 Read two chapters.
2 day(s) shown.
```
sections.Notes:
- Days are kept in date order even if you add an entry for an earlier day.
- `--search` exits with 1 when nothing matches, which is handy in scripts.
- Anything above the first dated heading (such as your `# Journal` title) is preserved.

tools.name: countdown-timer
tools.summary: Count down to a date, a clock time or a duration like 90s, 25m or 1h30m.

schema.description: Count down to a date or duration.

arguments.help: pretend it is this moment, e.g. '2026-01-01 09:00'

sections.Purpose: See how long is left until a deadline, a holiday or the end of a short timer. Give it a date, a date with a time, or a duration such as `90s`, `25m` or `1h30m`.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python countdown_timer.py TARGET [--live] [--now 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM']
```
`TARGET` can be `2026-12-25`, `'2026-12-25 18:00'` or a duration (`2d 3h`, `45m`, `90s`). By default it prints the remaining time once. `--live` keeps updating every second until the time is up (Ctrl+C to stop). `--now` pretends it is another moment, which is useful for testing.
sections.Notes:
- Dates without a time mean midnight at the start of that day, in your local time zone.
- A target in the past is reported as "... ago" instead of failing.
- Live mode needs a real terminal because it redraws a single line.

tools.name: timezone-converter
tools.summary: Convert a time between time zones, handling daylight saving time correctly.

schema.description: Convert a time between time zones.

arguments.help: date for the conversion, YYYY-MM-DD (default: today)
search zone names instead, e.g. london

sections.Purpose: Work out what time a meeting is for everyone. Give a time in one zone and see it in several others, including whether it lands on the next or previous day. Daylight saving changes are handled for the date you choose.
sections.Install:
Needs the `tzdata` package so Windows has a time zone database (it does nothing harmful on Linux or macOS):
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python timezone_converter.py TIME [--from ZONE] [--to ZONE ...] [--date YYYY-MM-DD]
python timezone_converter.py --find london
```
`TIME` can be `14:30` or `2:30pm`. Zone names look like `Europe/London` or `America/New_York`. `--find` searches the zone names.
sections.Example:
```bash
python timezone_converter.py 12:00 --from Europe/London --to America/New_York Asia/Tokyo --date 2026-01-15
```
```
Thu 2026-01-15 12:00 Europe/London (+0000)
  Thu 2026-01-15 07:00  America/New_York (-0500)
  Thu 2026-01-15 21:00  Asia/Tokyo (+0900)
  Thu 2026-01-15 17:30  Asia/Kolkata (+0530)
```
sections.Notes:
- The date matters: the same clock time converts differently in summer and winter.
- Unknown zone names stop with a message that suggests `--find`.
- Read-only.

tools.name: quick-notes
tools.summary: Capture and search quick notes from the shell. Notes live in a small JSON file.

arguments.help: note text, search word or note number
timestamp to record instead of now (for testing)

sections.Purpose: Jot something down without leaving the terminal, then find it again. Add `#tags` inside a note and filter by them later.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python quick_notes.py add TEXT...            # e.g. add Buy oat milk #errands
python quick_notes.py list [--tag TAG]
python quick_notes.py search WORD [--tag TAG]
python quick_notes.py tags
python quick_notes.py delete NUMBER
```
Notes are stored in a small JSON file (default `~/.quick-notes.json`, change it with `--file`). That file is the tool's own storage, so changes are saved straight away.
sections.Example:
```bash
python quick_notes.py list --tag errands --file notes.json
```
```
#3   2026-01-06 11:03  Call the bank about the card #errands #money
#1   2026-01-05 09:10  Buy oat milk #errands
2 note(s).
```
sections.Notes:
- Newest notes come first. Note numbers are never reused.
- A tag is `#` followed by letters, digits, `_` or `-`; matching ignores case.
- `search` exits with 1 when nothing matches.

tools.name: expense-logger
tools.summary: Log expenses to a CSV file and see totals by category. Money is handled exactly.

arguments.help: only this month, YYYY-MM (list and summary)
date for a new expense, YYYY-MM-DD (default: today)

sections.Purpose: Know where the money goes. Log each purchase in a second, then see totals per category for any month. Everything is stored in a plain CSV file that opens in a spreadsheet.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python expense_logger.py add AMOUNT CATEGORY [NOTE ...] [--date YYYY-MM-DD]
python expense_logger.py list [--month YYYY-MM]
python expense_logger.py summary [--month YYYY-MM]
```
The default file is `~/expenses.csv` (change it with `--file`). This file is the tool's own storage, so `add` writes to it straight away.
sections.Example:
```bash
python expense_logger.py summary --month 2026-01 --file expenses.csv
```
```
groceries       100.85  #################
transport        12.00  ##
coffee            4.50  #
total           117.35  (4 expenses)
```
sections.Notes:
- Amounts use exact decimal arithmetic, so 0.10 + 0.20 is exactly 0.30.
- Currency symbols and thousands commas in the amount are accepted and ignored.
- Categories are lowercased so `Coffee` and `coffee` are the same.

tools.name: break-reminder
tools.summary: Nag you to take a break every N minutes, right in the terminal. No desktop app needed.

arguments.help: your own reminder text (default: rotating tips)
read --every as minutes or seconds (seconds suits a demo)
clock time the session starts, HH:MM (default: now)

sections.Purpose: Long stretches at a screen are hard on your back and eyes. This prints a gentle reminder in your terminal every half hour (or whatever you choose), with a different tip each time. There is no desktop app to install.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python break_reminder.py [--every MIN] [--total MIN] [--message TEXT]
                         [--plan] [--start HH:MM] [--unit minutes|seconds] [--no-bell]
```
Run it in a spare terminal tab. `--plan` lists the reminder times and exits. `--unit seconds` makes the interval seconds for a quick demo. Press Ctrl+C to stop.
sections.Example:
```bash
python break_reminder.py --plan --start 09:00 --every 45 --total 180
```
```
09:45  Stand up and stretch your legs.
10:30  Drink some water.
11:15  Look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds.
12:00  Roll your shoulders and unclench your jaw.
4 reminder(s) over 180 minutes, every 45 minutes.
```
sections.Notes:
- Reminders start one interval after the start time and stop after `--total` minutes.
- Without `--message` the five built-in tips rotate; with it, your text repeats.
- The bell may be muted by your terminal settings; add `--no-bell` to silence it.

tools.name: weekly-planner
tools.summary: Generate a weekly planner in markdown: goals, a section per day and a review.

schema.description: Generate a weekly planner in markdown.

arguments.help: any date in the week, YYYY-MM-DD (default: next Monday)
write the planner to this file
really write --output (default only prints the planner)

sections.Purpose: Start each week with a clear page: a goals checklist, a section for every day with to-do lines ready to fill in, and a short review at the end. The result is plain markdown that works in any notes app, including Notion and Obsidian.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python weekly_planner.py [--week-of YYYY-MM-DD] [--goals GOAL ...] [--weekend] [--slots N]
                         [-o FILE --apply]
```
Without `--week-of` it plans the coming Monday. Any date in a week works, and the planner always starts on that week's Monday. The planner is printed; to save it, pass `-o` with `--apply` (an existing file is never overwritten).
sections.Example:
```bash
python weekly_planner.py --week-of 2026-01-05 --goals "Finish report" "Gym 3 times"
```
```
# Week of 05 Jan 2026
*05 Jan to 09 Jan*
sections.Notes:
- Wrap goals containing spaces in quotes.
- `--weekend` adds Saturday and Sunday; `--slots` changes the number of to-do lines per day.
- Paste the output into a Notion page and the checkboxes become real to-dos.

tools.name: standup-generator
tools.summary: Build a daily standup (yesterday / today / blockers) from your git commits.

schema.description: Generate a daily standup from git commits.

arguments.help: read a saved git log file instead of running git
only commits whose author name/email match
treat this date as today, YYYY-MM-DD

sections.Purpose: Answer "what did you do yesterday?" in seconds. It reads your recent git commits and writes a standup with yesterday's work, today's work so far and a blockers line. Mondays and weekends look back to Friday, and commit subjects such as `feat(ui): add dark mode` are tidied into `Add dark mode`.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+, and `git` on your PATH for real repositories.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python standup_generator.py [--repo PATH] [--author TEXT] [--today YYYY-MM-DD] [--raw]
python standup_generator.py --log git-log.txt --author ada
```
By default it runs `git log` in the repository. To work from a saved history (for example on a machine without git, or on the website), save one with:
```bash
git log --date=short --pretty=format:'@@%H%x1f%an%x1f%ae%x1f%ad%x1f%s' > git-log.txt
```
`--author` matches part of the author's name or email.
sections.Example:
```bash
python standup_generator.py --log git-log.txt --author Ada --today 2026-01-13
```
```
Standup for Tue 2026-01-13 (Ada)

Yesterday (Mon 2026-01-12):
- Update install guide (c3d4e5f)
- Split the router into modules (e5f6a7b)

Today so far:
- Add password reset flow (a1b2c3d)

Blockers:
- None
```
sections.Notes:
- Read-only. It never changes your repository.
- Without `--author` the standup includes everyone's commits, which suits a team summary.
- `--raw` keeps the original commit subjects instead of tidying them.

tools.name: git-log-summarizer
tools.summary: Summarize git history: commits per author, per week and per type of change.

schema.description: Summarize commits by author, week and type.

arguments.help: read a saved git log file instead of running git
only commits after this date, e.g. 2026-01-01 (git mode)

sections.Purpose: Get the shape of a project's history at a glance: who committed how much, how activity moves from week to week, and what kinds of changes dominate (features, fixes, docs). Types are read from conventional commit prefixes such as `feat:` and `fix:`.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+, and `git` on your PATH for real repositories.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python git_log_summarizer.py [--repo PATH] [--since YYYY-MM-DD]
python git_log_summarizer.py --log git-log.txt
```
By default it runs `git log` in the repository. To use a saved history instead (for example on the website), create one with:
```bash
git log --date=short --pretty=format:'@@%H%x1f%an%x1f%ae%x1f%ad%x1f%s' > git-log.txt
```
sections.Example:
```bash
python git_log_summarizer.py --log git-log.txt
```
```
12 commit(s) by 3 author(s)

By author
     5  Ada Lovelace
     4  Lin Chen
     3  Max Weber

By week            Ada       Lin       Max   total
  2026-W02         2         3         2       7
  2026-W03         3         1         1       5

By type
     5  feat
     2  fix
```
sections.Notes:
- Weeks are ISO weeks (they start on Monday), shown as `YYYY-Www`.
- Commits without a `type:` prefix are counted as `other`.
- Read-only.

tools.name: commit-message-linter
tools.summary: Check commit messages against a format: conventional commits, length and tidiness.

arguments.help: check a saved git log file

sections.Purpose: Keep commit history readable. It checks subjects against the conventional-commits format (`feat: add login`, `fix(cart): handle empty cart`), a length limit, trailing periods and vague messages such as `wip`. Use it on recent commits, on a saved log, or on a single message from a git hook.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+, and `git` on your PATH for real repositories.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python commit_message_linter.py [--repo PATH] [-n COUNT] [--style conventional|free] [--max-length N]
python commit_message_linter.py --message "feat: add login"
python commit_message_linter.py --log git-log.txt
```
By default it lints the last 20 commits in the repository. To use a saved history instead (for example on the website), create one with:
```bash
git log --date=short --pretty=format:'@@%H%x1f%an%x1f%ae%x1f%ad%x1f%s' > git-log.txt
```
The exit code is 1 when any message has a problem, so it can run in CI or a `commit-msg` hook.
sections.Example:
```bash
python commit_message_linter.py --log git-log.txt
```
```
d4e5f6a  wip stuff
        - not in the form 'type: description' (types: feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, perf, test, build, ci, chore, revert)
a7b8c9d  Fixed bug.
        - subject ends with a period
        - not in the form 'type: description' (types: feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, perf, test, build, ci, chore, revert)
e1f2a3b  feat: add a very long subject line that goes well beyond the...
        - subject is 100 characters (limit 72)
12 message(s) checked, 3 with problems.
```
sections.Notes:
- Allowed types: feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, perf, test, build, ci, chore, revert.
- `--style free` skips the type rule and only checks length, spacing and vagueness.
- Read-only.

tools.name: git-author-stats
tools.summary: Count commits and changed lines per author in a git repository.

arguments.help: read a saved git log --numstat file

sections.Purpose: See who did what in a repository: commits, share of the total, lines added and deleted, how many different days each person committed, and when they were active. Handy for retrospectives and for crediting contributors.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+, and `git` on your PATH for real repositories.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python git_author_stats.py [--repo PATH] [--by name|email] [--sort commits|lines]
python git_author_stats.py --log git-log.txt
```
By default it runs `git log --numstat` in the repository. To use a saved history instead (for example on the website), create one with:
```bash
git log --numstat --date=short --pretty=format:'@@%H%x1f%an%x1f%ae%x1f%ad%x1f%s' > git-log.txt
```
sections.Example:
```bash
python git_author_stats.py --log git-log.txt
```
```
author             commits  share   added  deleted  days  active
Ada Lovelace             5    42%     883       87     4  2026-01-05 to 2026-01-13
Lin Chen                 4    33%     261        6     4  2026-01-05 to 2026-01-12
Max Weber                3    25%      13        8     3  2026-01-06 to 2026-01-12
12 commit(s), 3 author(s).
```
sections.Notes:
- Use `--by email` when the same person commits under several names.
- Line counts are not a measure of quality, and binary files are not counted.
- Read-only.

tools.name: todo-comment-finder
tools.summary: List TODO, FIXME and similar comments across a code base.

sections.Purpose: Turn scattered reminders in your code into a list. It finds `TODO`, `FIXME`, `HACK` and `XXX` comments in any language that uses `#`, `//`, `/* */`, `<!-- -->`, `--` or `;` comments, reports the file and line, and counts them by tag.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python todo_comment_finder.py [FOLDER] [--tags TODO FIXME ...] [--owner NAME]
```
`--owner` keeps only comments written like `TODO(ada): ...`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python todo_comment_finder.py demo-project
```
```
src/app.js:2  TODO  add rate limiting to the API
src/app.js:4  FIXME  crashes when the cart is empty
src/app.js:7  HACK  temporary workaround for the legacy client
src/utils.js:1  TODO (ada)  cache the results of this lookup
src/utils.js:3  XXX  remove before the 2.0 release
tests/app.test.js:2  TODO  cover the empty cart case
6 comment(s) found: 3 TODO, 1 FIXME, 1 HACK, 1 XXX.
```
sections.Notes:
- Matching ignores letter case, but the tag must sit inside a comment, so strings containing the word TODO are not reported.
- `.git`, `node_modules`, virtual environments, build folders, binary files and files over 1 MB are skipped.
- Read-only.

tools.name: gitignore-generator
tools.summary: Generate a .gitignore for the languages, tools and operating systems you use.

arguments.help: one or more of: dotenv, dotnet, go, java, jetbrains, linux, logs, macos, node, python, rust, vscode, windows
add only missing lines to an existing --output file
really write --output (default only prints the result)

sections.Purpose: Start a repository with a sensible `.gitignore` in seconds. Pick the languages, editors and operating systems you use and get one combined file with no repeated lines.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python gitignore_generator.py STACK [STACK ...] [-o .gitignore --apply] [--append]
```
Available stacks: python, node, java, go, rust, dotnet, dotenv, macos, windows, linux, vscode, jetbrains, logs. The result is printed; to save it pass `-o` with `--apply`. An existing file is never overwritten unless you add `--append`, which adds only the lines it doesn't already have.
sections.Example:
```bash
python gitignore_generator.py python dotenv macos
```
```
# python
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
*.egg-info/
.venv/
venv/
build/
dist/
.pytest_cache/
.mypy_cache/
.ruff_cache/
.coverage
htmlcov/

# dotenv
.env
.env.*
!.env.example

# macos
.DS_Store
.AppleDouble
.LSOverride
._*
```
sections.Notes:
- `dotenv` ignores `.env` files but keeps `.env.example` tracked.
- Lines already ignored by an earlier stack are not repeated.
- Check the result before committing; every project has its own odd files.

tools.name: repo-readme-generator
tools.summary: Draft a README for a project by looking at the files it contains.

schema.description: Draft a README from a project folder.

arguments.help: write the README to this file
really write --output (default only prints the draft)

sections.Purpose: Get a README draft instead of a blank page. It looks at the project folder and writes a starting point with the project name and description, the main languages, install and run commands, a short folder tree and the license.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python repo_readme_generator.py [FOLDER] [-o README.md --apply]
```
The draft is printed. To save it pass `-o` with `--apply`; an existing file is never overwritten.
sections.Example:
```bash
python repo_readme_generator.py demo-project
```
````
# shop-demo

A tiny demo storefront

Built with JavaScript.
sections.Getting started:
```bash
npm install
npm start
npm run test
npm run build
```
sections.Project structure:
```
src/
  app.js
  utils.js
tests/
  app.test.js
LICENSE
package.json
```
sections.Notes:
- It understands `package.json` (name, description, scripts, license), `requirements.txt` and `pyproject.toml`.
- It is a draft: fill in the description, usage examples and screenshots yourself.
- `.git`, `node_modules`, virtual environments and build folders are left out of the tree.

tools.name: changelog-generator
tools.summary: Build a changelog section from conventional commits (feat, fix, docs ...).

arguments.help: read a saved git log file instead of running git
only commits after this date or tag (git mode)
add the section to this CHANGELOG file
really update --output (default only prints the section)

sections.Purpose: Write release notes from your commit history. Commits that follow the conventional format (`feat: ...`, `fix(scope): ...`, `feat!: ...`) are grouped into Features, Bug fixes, Documentation and so on, with breaking changes called out first.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+, and `git` on your PATH for real repositories.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python changelog_generator.py [--repo PATH] [--since TAG_OR_DATE] [--version 1.2.0]
                              [--date YYYY-MM-DD] [-o CHANGELOG.md --apply]
python changelog_generator.py --log git-log.txt
```
By default it reads `git log` from the repository; `--since v1.1.0` limits it to commits after that tag. The section is printed; with `-o` and `--apply` it is added under the `# Changelog` title, above older releases. To use a saved history instead (for example on the website), create one with:
```bash
git log --date=short --pretty=format:'@@%H%x1f%an%x1f%ae%x1f%ad%x1f%s' > git-log.txt
```
sections.Example:
```bash
python changelog_generator.py --log git-log.txt --version 1.2.0 --date 2026-01-14
```
```
sections.[1.2.0] - 2026-01-14:
### BREAKING CHANGES

- drop support for Node 16 (d0e1f2a)

### Features

- add password reset flow (a1b2c3d)
- **ui:** add dark mode toggle (f6a7b8c)
- export orders as CSV (c9d0e1f)
- add a very long subject line that goes well beyond the recommended seventy two character limit (e1f2a3b)
- initial project setup (f2a3b4c)

### Bug fixes

- handle empty cart in checkout (b2c3d4e)
- drop support for Node 16 (d0e1f2a)

### Refactoring

- split the router into modules (e5f6a7b)

### Documentation

- update install guide (c3d4e5f)

### Chores

- bump dependencies (b8c9d0e)
```
sections.Notes:
- Commits without a recognised `type:` prefix are counted and left out rather than guessed at.
- Each entry ends with the short commit hash so you can trace it.
- Review the result: a changelog is for people, so reword anything unclear.

tools.name: branch-lister
tools.summary: List local git branches with how long ago each was last committed to.

arguments.help: read a saved for-each-ref file instead of git
treat this date as today, YYYY-MM-DD (for testing)

sections.Purpose: See which branches are alive and which have been forgotten. Every local branch is listed newest first with its last commit date, a friendly age (`4d ago`, `3mo ago`), the author and the last commit message, and branches that haven't moved in a while are marked `STALE`.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+, and `git` on your PATH for real repositories.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python branch_lister.py [--repo PATH] [--stale-days N]
python branch_lister.py --refs branches.txt [--today YYYY-MM-DD]
```
By default it asks git for the local branches. To use a saved list instead (for example on the website), create one with:
```bash
git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short)%1f%(committerdate:short)%1f%(authorname)%1f%(subject)' refs/heads > branches.txt
```
`--stale-days` sets how many days of silence count as stale (default 90).
sections.Example:
```bash
python branch_lister.py --refs branches.txt --today 2026-01-13
```
```
main               2026-01-13     today  Ada Lovelace  feat: add password reset flow
feature/dark-mode  2026-01-09    4d ago  Lin Chen      feat(ui): add dark mode toggle
release/1.0        2025-12-15    4w ago  Ada Lovelace  chore: prepare release 1.0
fix/cart-bug       2025-11-20    7w ago  Lin Chen      fix: cart total rounding
old/experiment     2025-06-02   7mo ago  Max Weber     try a new layout  STALE
5 branch(es), 1 older than 90 days.
```
sections.Notes:
- Read-only: it never deletes or changes a branch. When you are ready to clean up, check `git branch --merged` first.
- `--today` pins the date, which makes the output repeatable.
- Ages are measured from each branch's last commit date.

tools.name: repo-size-reporter
tools.summary: Report how big a repository is and which files and file types take the most space.

arguments.help: how many big files to list (5)
also count node_modules and virtual environments

sections.Purpose: Find out why a repository is heavy. It reports the size of the working tree and of the `.git` history separately, lists the biggest files, and breaks the total down by file type, so an accidentally committed video or data dump stands out.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python repo_size_reporter.py [FOLDER] [-n TOP] [--include-deps]
```
`node_modules` and virtual environments are skipped unless you pass `--include-deps`. If the folder contains a `.git` directory its size is shown on its own line.
sections.Example:
```bash
python repo_size_reporter.py demo-project
```
```
Working tree: 723 B in 5 file(s)

Largest 5 file(s):
      254 B  src/app.js
      206 B  package.json
      128 B  src/utils.js
       93 B  tests/app.test.js
       42 B  LICENSE

By file type:
  .js         3 file(s)      475 B   66%
  .json       1 file(s)      206 B   28%
  (none)      1 file(s)       42 B    6%
```
sections.Notes:
- Read-only.
- A very large `.git` size usually means big files were committed at some point, even if they were deleted later; they remain in the history.
- Sizes are the files' byte sizes, not disk blocks, so they can differ slightly from your file manager.

tools.name: pdf-merger
tools.summary: Merge several PDF files into one, in the order you give them.

arguments.help: PDF files, in the order to merge
add a bookmark for each source file
really write the merged file (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Combine several PDFs into one document, in exactly the order you list them. Handy for bundling scans, chapters or receipts into a single file. Optional bookmarks make it easy to jump between the original parts.
sections.Install:
Needs `pypdf`:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python pdf_merger.py FILE.pdf FILE.pdf [...] [-o merged.pdf] [--bookmarks] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it shows each file's page count and what the result would hold. Pass `--apply` to write the merged file. An existing output file is never overwritten.
sections.Example:
```bash
python pdf_merger.py report.pdf handbook.pdf -o combined.pdf --bookmarks
```
```
report.pdf: 3 page(s)
handbook.pdf: 5 page(s)
Dry run: would write combined.pdf with 8 page(s). Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- The source files are never changed.
- A file that isn't a readable PDF (or is password protected) stops the run with a message naming it.
- To split a PDF again, see `pdf-splitter`.

tools.name: pdf-splitter
tools.summary: Split a PDF by page ranges, or into fixed-size parts (one page each by default).

arguments.help: pages to extract into ONE file, e.g. 1-3,5,8-
one file per N pages (1 = one per page)
really write the files (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Pull pages out of a PDF. Either extract a selection (such as pages 1 to 3 and 5) into one new file, or break the whole document into parts of a fixed size, down to one file per page.
sections.Install:
Needs `pypdf`:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python pdf_splitter.py FILE.pdf --pages 1-3,5,8- [-o OUTDIR] [--apply]
python pdf_splitter.py FILE.pdf --every N [-o OUTDIR] [--apply]
```
Use exactly one of `--pages` or `--every`. Page numbers start at 1, and `8-` means page 8 to the end. Dry run by default: it lists the files it would create. Pass `--apply` to write them next to the original (or into `-o`).
sections.Example:
```bash
python pdf_splitter.py handbook.pdf --every 2
```
```
handbook_part001.pdf  (pages 1-2 of 5)
handbook_part002.pdf  (pages 3-4 of 5)
handbook_part003.pdf  (page 5 of 5)
Would write 3 file(s). Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- The original PDF is never changed.
- Output names are `<name>_pages_<ranges>.pdf` or `<name>_part001.pdf`, `<name>_part002.pdf` and so on.
- A page number outside the document stops the run with a clear message.

tools.name: pdf-page-counter
tools.summary: Count the pages in PDF files and folders of PDFs.

sections.Purpose: Find out how many pages a stack of PDFs adds up to, for example before printing, estimating translation work or checking an upload limit. It lists each file with its page count and size, then the grand total.
sections.Install:
Needs `pypdf`:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python pdf_page_counter.py PATH [PATH ...] [-r]
```
`PATH` can be PDF files or folders. Folders are searched for `.pdf` files, including subfolders when you pass `-r`. The exit code is 1 if any file had to be skipped.
sections.Example:
```bash
python pdf_page_counter.py report.pdf handbook.pdf scan_0001.pdf
```
```
report.pdf         3 page(s)     1.4 KB
handbook.pdf       5 page(s)     2.0 KB
scan_0001.pdf      1 page(s)      679 B
3 PDF(s), 9 page(s) in total.
```
sections.Notes:
- Password-protected and damaged files are reported as skipped instead of stopping the run.
- Sizes are the files' sizes on disk.
- Read-only.

tools.name: pdf-text-extractor
tools.summary: Extract the text from PDF files, to the screen or into .txt files.

arguments.help: characters of each file to show (0 = all; default 600)
really write the .txt files (default only prints a preview)

sections.Purpose: Get the text out of PDFs so you can search it, quote it or feed it to other tools. By default it prints a short preview of each file; with `--apply` it saves each PDF's full text as a `.txt` file.
sections.Install:
Needs `pypdf`:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python pdf_text_extractor.py FILE.pdf [FILE.pdf ...] [--markers] [--preview N] [-o OUTDIR --apply]
```
`--markers` adds a `--- page N ---` line before each page. `--preview 0` shows the whole text. Without `--apply` nothing is written. With it, `report.pdf` becomes `report.txt` next to the PDF (or in `-o`).
sections.Example:
```bash
python pdf_text_extractor.py report.pdf --markers
```
```
== report.pdf: 3 page(s), 42 word(s)
--- page 1 ---
Quarterly report
Page one: summary of results.
Revenue grew 12 percent.

--- page 2 ---
Page two: details
Costs were flat compared with last quarter.

--- page 3 ---
Page three: outlook
We expect steady growth next quarter.

Preview only. Use --apply to save .txt files.
```
sections.Notes:
- This reads the text layer of the PDF. A scan made of pictures has no text layer, and the tool says so instead of printing nothing.
- Password-protected or damaged files are reported and skipped; the exit code is then 1.
- Layout (columns, tables) is flattened to plain text, so check anything that depends on position.

tools.name: pdf-rotator
tools.summary: Rotate all or some pages of a PDF, writing the result to a new file.

arguments.help: pages to rotate, e.g. 1-3,5 (default: all pages)
really write the file (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Fix sideways scans. Turn every page of a PDF, or just the ones you choose, by 90, 180 or 270 degrees clockwise. The result is saved as a new file and the original stays untouched.
sections.Install:
Needs `pypdf`:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python pdf_rotator.py FILE.pdf --angle 90|180|270 [--pages 1-3,5] [-o OUTPUT] [--apply]
```
Without `--pages` every page is rotated. Dry run by default: it tells you what would happen. Pass `--apply` to write `<name>_rotated.pdf` (or the file you name with `-o`). An existing output file is never overwritten.
sections.Example:
```bash
python pdf_rotator.py handbook.pdf --angle 90 --pages 2-3
```
```
handbook.pdf: rotate 2 of 5 page(s) by 90 degrees
Dry run: would write handbook_rotated.pdf. Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- Rotation is clockwise and adds to any rotation a page already has.
- Page numbers start at 1; `3-` means page 3 to the end.
- The page content is not re-rendered, so there is no loss of quality.

tools.name: markdown-to-pdf
tools.summary: Turn a markdown file into a clean, readable PDF.

arguments.help: really write the PDF (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Turn notes, READMEs and reports written in markdown into a tidy A4 PDF you can print or share. It handles headings, paragraphs, bullet and numbered lists, code blocks and horizontal rules, and tidies links, bold and italics into plain text.
sections.Install:
Needs `fpdf2`:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python markdown_to_pdf.py FILE.md [-o OUTPUT.pdf] [--apply]
```
