Dry run by default: it renders in memory and reports how many pages the PDF would have. Pass `--apply` to write `<name>.pdf` (or the file you name with `-o`). An existing file is never overwritten.
sections.Example:
```bash
python markdown_to_pdf.py README.md
```
```
README.md: 9 block(s) -> 1 page(s), 1237 bytes
Dry run: would write README.pdf. Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- It uses the PDF standard fonts, which only cover Western European characters; anything else is replaced with `?`. Curly quotes and dashes are converted to plain ones.
- Tables and images in the markdown are not rendered, only their text.
- For heavily styled documents, a browser's "print to PDF" on rendered HTML will look richer.

tools.name: invoice-renamer
tools.summary: Rename invoice PDFs to 'date_vendor_number.pdf' using the text inside them.

schema.description: Rename invoice PDFs from their contents.

arguments.help: really rename the files (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Turn a folder of anonymous scans such as `scan_0001.pdf` into files you can find again: `2026-01-15_ACME-Supplies-Ltd_INV-1042.pdf`. It reads the text on the first pages, finds the invoice date, the vendor (the first line) and the invoice number, and builds the name from them.
sections.Install:
Needs `pypdf`:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python invoice_renamer.py FOLDER [--pattern "{date}_{vendor}_{number}"] [--monthfirst] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it shows each rename. Pass `--apply` to rename the files. Dates like `12/02/2026` are read day first (12 February); add `--monthfirst` for US style. The pattern can use any of `{date}`, `{vendor}` and `{number}`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python invoice_renamer.py .
```
```
skip handbook.pdf: couldn't find everything the pattern needs (found vendor=Handbook chapter 1)
skip report.pdf: couldn't find everything the pattern needs (found vendor=Quarterly report)
scan_0001.pdf -> 2026-01-15_ACME-Supplies-Ltd_INV-1042.pdf
scan_0002.pdf -> 2026-02-12_Blue-Sky-Hosting_BS-7781.pdf
Would rename 2 invoice(s), skipped 2. Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- Invoices where a needed part can't be found are skipped and left alone, with a note of what was found.
- It never overwrites an existing file, and two invoices that would get the same name are not both renamed.
- Scanned images with no text layer can't be read (they need OCR first).

tools.name: pdf-metadata-viewer

sections.Install:
Needs `pypdf`:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python pdf_metadata_viewer.py FILE.pdf [FILE.pdf ...] [--json]
```
sections.Example:
```bash
python pdf_metadata_viewer.py report.pdf handbook.pdf
```

  encrypted  False
  pages      3
  title      Quarterly Report

```
sections.Notes:
- Only fields that are present are shown. Many PDFs have no title or author.

tools.name: docx-text-extractor
tools.summary: Pull plain text (or simple markdown) out of Word .docx files without Word.

arguments.help: keep headings, bullets and tables as markdown
really write the files (default only prints the text)

sections.Purpose: Read Word documents without Word. It pulls out the text in order, including bullet points and tables, and can keep headings, bullets and tables as markdown so the result drops straight into notes, a wiki or a search index.

sections.Usage:
```bash
python docx_text_extractor.py FILE.docx [FILE.docx ...] [--markdown] [-o OUTDIR --apply]
```
The text is printed; with `--apply` each document is saved as `<name>.txt` (or `<name>.md` with `--markdown`) next to it or in `-o`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python docx_text_extractor.py contract.docx --markdown
```
```

- Confidentiality applies to both parties.

| Item | Price |
| --- | --- |
| Consulting | $1,200 |

```
sections.Notes:
- Only the modern `.docx` format is supported, not the old `.doc`.
- Headers, footers, footnotes and text boxes are not included, only the main body.
- It never opens the file in Word, so macros cannot run. Very large documents are refused.

tools.name: images-to-pdf
tools.summary: Combine images into a single PDF, one image per page.

arguments.help: a4 pages with the image centred, or pages sized to each image
really write the PDF (default is a dry run)

Needs Pillow (and `pypdf` only for the tests):

pip install -r requirements.txt
```

python images_to_pdf.py IMAGE_OR_FOLDER [...] [--size a4|fit] [-o images.pdf] [--apply]
```
A folder contributes its images sorted by name; individual files keep the order you list them. Dry run by default: it lists the pages. Pass `--apply` to write the PDF. An existing output file is never overwritten.

```bash
python images_to_pdf.py "Holiday Photo 01.JPG" "Holiday Photo 02.JPG" logo.png -o album.pdf
```

Holiday Photo 02.JPG: 300x200
logo.png: 240x120
3 page(s), a4 size
Dry run: would write album.pdf. Use --apply to do it.
```

- Transparent images are flattened onto white, and photos are turned upright using their EXIF orientation.
- On A4 pages, wide images get landscape pages and tall ones portrait pages, with a small margin.
- Unreadable files are skipped with a message.

tools.name: bulk-url-checker
tools.summary: Check the HTTP status of many URLs at once: working, redirecting or broken.

schema.description: Check the status of many URLs.

arguments.help: URLs, or text files with one URL per line
only list what would be checked (no requests are made)

sections.Purpose: Find out which links in a list still work. Every URL gets its HTTP status, response time and the final address after redirects, and the run exits with 1 if anything is broken, so it works in scheduled checks and CI.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python bulk_url_checker.py URL_OR_FILE [URL_OR_FILE ...] [--plan] [--timeout SEC] [--workers N]
```
Pass URLs directly or text files with one URL per line (`#` starts a comment). Duplicates are removed (`https://Example.com` and `https://example.com/` count as one). `--plan` only lists what would be checked and sends nothing. Requests run several at a time, politely, with a `HEAD` request first and `GET` only if the server refuses `HEAD`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python bulk_url_checker.py urls.txt --plan
```
```
SKIP  not an http(s) URL: not a url
WOULD CHECK  https://example.com/
WOULD CHECK  https://www.python.org/
WOULD CHECK  http://example.org/page?utm_source=news&id=7
Would check 3 URL(s); 1 invalid, 2 duplicate(s) removed.
```
sections.Notes:
- Checking URLs needs network access, so the website demo can only run the `--plan` mode; run the real check on your own computer.
- Only check sites you are allowed to; keep `--workers` low for small servers.
- A timeout or connection failure is reported as `FAIL` with the reason.

tools.name: link-extractor
tools.summary: List the links on a web page (a URL or a saved .html file), sorted into internal and external.

schema.description: Extract the links from a web page.

arguments.help: a page URL, or a saved .html file
page address, to resolve links in a saved file

sections.Purpose: See every link on a page at a glance. It lists each unique link with its visible text, tells internal links from external ones, and marks links with `rel="nofollow"`. Useful for audits, migrations and finding what a page points to.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python link_extractor.py URL_OR_FILE [--base PAGE_URL] [--only internal|external]
```
Give a page address to download it, or a saved `.html` file (add `--base` so relative links such as `/products` can be turned into full addresses and classified). Links like `mailto:`, `tel:`, `javascript:` and `#anchors` are skipped, and repeated links appear once.
sections.Example:
```bash
python link_extractor.py page.html --base https://example.com/
```
```
internal  https://example.com/products  'Products'
internal  https://example.com/about.html  'About us'
internal  https://example.com/docs  'Docs'
external  https://partner.test/page  'partner' [nofollow]
4 unique link(s): 3 internal, 1 external.
```
sections.Notes:
- Downloading a page needs network access. The website demo works from the sample saved page; with a real URL, run it on your own computer.
- Pages are read up to 2 MB. Links added later by JavaScript are not seen, because the page is not run.
- Read-only.

tools.name: robots-checker
tools.summary: Check whether a URL or path is allowed by a site's robots.txt, for a given crawler name.

arguments.help: a saved robots.txt to check against

sections.Purpose: Before scraping or crawling a site, find out what its `robots.txt` allows. Give it URLs and it tells you which are allowed or blocked for your crawler name, which rule decided it, the requested crawl delay and any sitemaps listed.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python robots_checker.py URL [URL ...] [--agent NAME]
python robots_checker.py PATH [PATH ...] --robots robots.txt [--agent NAME]
```
With full URLs it downloads each site's `robots.txt` once. With `--robots` it uses a saved file instead and you can give plain paths such as `/private/page`. The exit code is 1 if anything is blocked.
sections.Example:
```bash
python robots_checker.py /private/public/page /private/secret /admin/panel /products --robots robots.txt
```
```
ALLOWED /private/public/page  (rule: Allow /private/public/)
BLOCKED /private/secret  (rule: Disallow /private)
BLOCKED /admin/panel  (rule: Disallow /admin/)
ALLOWED /products
Crawl-delay for *: 5 seconds between requests.
Sitemaps: https://example.com/sitemap.xml
```
sections.Notes:
- It follows the standard rules: the most specific (longest) matching rule wins, `*` and a trailing `$` are supported, and a crawler-specific group beats the `*` group.
- A missing `robots.txt` (404) means everything is allowed.
- Fetching a real `robots.txt` needs network access; the website demo uses the sample file.
- This is a courtesy check, not permission: sites can also have terms of use.

tools.name: rss-digest
tools.summary: Turn RSS and Atom feeds into a short markdown digest of the newest items.

schema.description: Make a markdown digest from feeds.

arguments.help: feed URLs or saved feed files
only items on or after this date, YYYY-MM-DD
save the digest to this file
really write --output (default only prints the digest)

sections.Purpose: Skim your feeds without opening a reader. It reads RSS and Atom feeds, picks the newest items from each, tidies the summaries (no HTML) and writes a short markdown digest you can read, paste into notes or email to yourself.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python rss_digest.py FEED [FEED ...] [--since YYYY-MM-DD] [--limit N] [-o digest.md --apply]
```
`FEED` is a feed URL or a saved feed file. By default it shows the 5 newest items per feed. The digest is printed; to save it pass `-o` with `--apply` (an existing file is never overwritten).
sections.Example:
```bash
python rss_digest.py feed.xml --since 2026-01-01 --limit 3
```
```
# Feed digest (3 item(s) from 1 feed(s))
sections.ACME Blog:
- **Launching widgets 2.0** (2026-01-13) - Faster, lighter and cheaper than ever. [read](https://example.com/blog/widgets-2)
- **How we test our widgets** (2026-01-12) - A look inside the lab. [read](https://example.com/blog/testing)
- **Holiday opening hours** (2026-01-02) - We are closed on public holidays. [read](https://example.com/blog/holidays)
```
sections.Notes:
- Downloading a feed needs network access; the website demo uses a sample feed file.
- Feeds that contain a DOCTYPE or entity definitions are refused, which protects against malicious XML.
- Items with no date are listed after dated ones and are left out when you use `--since`.

tools.name: header-inspector
tools.summary: Show the HTTP response headers for a URL (or a saved header dump) with plain-English notes.

arguments.help: a URL, or a saved header dump (e.g. from curl -I)

sections.Purpose: See what a web server says about itself. It prints a URL's HTTP response headers in a tidy table and adds plain-English notes: the content type and size, how long browsers may cache it, where it redirects, what software it announces, how many cookies it sets and whether HSTS (forced HTTPS) is on.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python header_inspector.py URL [--follow]
python header_inspector.py saved-headers.txt
```
For a URL it sends one `HEAD` request and shows the first response, so a redirect shows its `Location` instead of being followed (add `--follow` to follow it). You can also read a saved dump, for example one made with `curl -I https://example.com > saved-headers.txt`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python header_inspector.py headers.txt
```
```
HTTP/2 200
  content-type               text/html; charset=utf-8
  server                     nginx/1.24
  cache-control              max-age=3600
  content-length             18211
  strict-transport-security  max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
  x-powered-by               Express
  set-cookie                 session=abc123; HttpOnly
  set-cookie                 theme=dark; Path=/
  x-content-type-options     nosniff

Notes:
  - Content: text/html (17.8 KB)
  - Caching: reusable for 1 hour
  - Server software announced: nginx/1.24
  - Technology revealed by X-Powered-By: Express
  - Sets 2 cookies
  - HSTS is on
```
sections.Notes:
- Requesting a URL needs network access; the website demo reads the sample file.
- Repeated headers such as `set-cookie` are all shown.
- Read-only. Only inspect sites you are allowed to; for a full security review see the security tools later in this challenge.

tools.name: page-title-fetcher
tools.summary: Get the title (and description) of web pages or saved .html files.

sections.Purpose: Turn a list of links into readable ones. For each page it reads the `<title>` (and optionally the meta description), so you can label bookmarks, build a link list for a document or spot pages with a missing title.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python page_title_fetcher.py SOURCE [SOURCE ...] [--description] [--csv]
```
A `SOURCE` is a page URL or a saved `.html` file. Pages are fetched several at a time, and only the first 256 KB of each is read. `--csv` prints a table you can open in a spreadsheet. The exit code is 1 if any page couldn't be read.
sections.Example:
```bash
python page_title_fetcher.py page.html page-two.html --description
```
```
ACME Widgets - Home  <-  page.html
    Quality widgets since 1999
Contact ACME  <-  page-two.html
2 of 2 page(s) read.
```
sections.Notes:
- Fetching URLs needs network access; the website demo reads the sample pages.
- Whitespace and line breaks inside titles are collapsed into single spaces.
- Titles set by JavaScript after the page loads are not seen.

tools.name: broken-link-finder
tools.summary: Find broken links on a web page: it reads the page, then checks every link on it.

schema.description: Find broken links on a page.

arguments.help: page URL, or a saved .html file (use --base with a file)
the page's address, to resolve relative links
only list the links that would be checked (no requests)
seconds to wait between requests, to be gentle on small sites

sections.Purpose: Catch dead links before your visitors do. It reads one page, collects every link on it and checks each one, listing the ones that return an error or don't answer at all. Handy for a website you maintain or documentation you publish.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python broken_link_finder.py PAGE_URL [--only internal|external] [--max N] [--delay SEC] [--plan]
python broken_link_finder.py saved.html --base https://example.com/ --plan
```
A saved `.html` file needs `--base` so relative links can be resolved. `--plan` lists the links that would be checked without sending any request. `--delay` waits between requests (and checks one at a time), which is kinder to small servers. The exit code is 1 when any link is broken.
sections.Example:
```bash
python broken_link_finder.py page.html --base https://example.com/ --plan
```
```
WOULD CHECK  https://example.com/products
WOULD CHECK  https://example.com/about.html
WOULD CHECK  https://example.com/docs
WOULD CHECK  https://partner.test/page
Would check 4 link(s) found on page.html.
```
sections.Notes:
- Checking links needs network access, so the website demo can only run `--plan`. Run the real check on your own computer.
- It checks the links on a single page, not a whole site, and stops at 100 links unless you raise `--max`.
- Only check sites you own or have permission to test. Some sites block automated checks and may report a working link as broken.

tools.name: sitemap-lister
tools.summary: List every URL in a sitemap.xml (a URL or a saved file), with last-modified dates.

schema.description: List the URLs in a sitemap.

arguments.help: only entries modified on or after YYYY-MM-DD
show at most this many (0 = all)

sections.Purpose: Get a clean list of every page a site publishes. It reads a `sitemap.xml` (or the sitemap index that points to several), shows each URL with its last-modified date and lets you filter by text or by date. A good starting point for audits, redirects and crawl planning.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python sitemap_lister.py SITEMAP [--contains TEXT] [--newer-than YYYY-MM-DD] [--limit N] [--csv]
```
`SITEMAP` is a sitemap URL or a saved `.xml` file. A sitemap index lists its child sitemaps; run the tool on each child to see the pages. `--csv` prints a table for a spreadsheet.
sections.Example:
```bash
python sitemap_lister.py sitemap.xml --newer-than 2025-12-01
```
```
2026-01-10  https://example.com/
2026-01-08  https://example.com/products
2025-12-20  https://example.com/products/widget-a
3 of 5 URL(s).
```
sections.Notes:
- Downloading a sitemap needs network access; the website demo reads the sample file.
- Dates are taken from the `lastmod` field, which not every site fills in; undated entries are hidden when you filter by date.
- Sitemaps containing a DOCTYPE or entity definitions are refused, which protects against malicious XML.

tools.name: url-expander
tools.summary: Follow redirects to see where a short link really goes, and strip tracking junk from URLs.

schema.description: Expand short links and clean tracking junk.

arguments.help: don't contact the server; only clean the URL

sections.Purpose: See where a link really goes before you click it. It follows the redirects of short links (bit.ly style) and tracking links one hop at a time, reports the final address and can strip tracking parameters such as `utm_source` and `fbclid` to give you a clean URL.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python url_expander.py URL [URL ...] [--clean] [--chain] [--max-hops N] [--no-follow]
```
By default each URL is followed through its redirects. `--chain` lists every hop with its HTTP status, `--clean` removes tracking parameters from the final address, and `--no-follow` skips the network entirely and only cleans the URL you gave. Redirect loops and over-long chains are detected and reported.
sections.Example:
```bash
python url_expander.py "http://Example.org/page?utm_source=news&id=7&fbclid=abc" --clean --no-follow
```
```
http://Example.org/page?utm_source=news&id=7&fbclid=abc
  -> http://example.org/page?id=7
```
sections.Notes:
- Following links needs network access, so the website demo runs the `--no-follow` cleaning mode. Following redirects works on your own computer.
- The tool only asks the server for headers and never downloads the page.
- Only the tracking parameters it knows are removed; the rest of the query string is kept as it was.

tools.name: ping-checker
tools.summary: Ping hosts and log the response times, or analyse saved ping output.

schema.description: Ping hosts and log response times.

arguments.help: host names or IP addresses to ping
analyse a saved ping output file instead
append each result to this CSV file

sections.Purpose: Keep an eye on your connection. It pings one or more hosts, summarises replies, packet loss and response times (min, average, max) and can log every check to a CSV so you can see when things got slow. It also reads saved ping output from Linux, macOS or Windows.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. It uses your system's `ping` command.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python ping_checker.py HOST [HOST ...] [-c COUNT] [--log pings.csv]
python ping_checker.py --parse ping-output.txt
```
Run it on a schedule (cron or Windows Task Scheduler) with `--log` to build up a history. The exit code is 1 if any host sent no replies at all. Host names are validated before anything is run, and nothing goes through a shell.
sections.Example:
```bash
python ping_checker.py --parse ping.txt
```
```
example.com              4/5 replies, 20% loss, min 11.9 / avg 21.1 / max 48.2 ms
```
sections.Notes:
- Pinging needs a real network and the `ping` program, so the website demo can only analyse saved output with `--parse`.
- Some networks block ping; "no replies" doesn't always mean the host is down.
- The CSV has the columns `timestamp, host, sent, received, loss_percent, min_ms, avg_ms, max_ms`.

tools.name: web-scraper
tools.summary: Scrape text or attributes from a page using CSS selectors, honoring robots.txt.

schema.description: Scrape a page with CSS selectors.

arguments.help: a page URL, or a saved .html file
what to scrape; repeat for several, e.g. title=h1 or 'a.buy'
read this attribute (href, src...) instead of the text
page address, to resolve relative links
robots.txt to check a URL against

sections.Purpose: Pull exactly the bits you want out of a web page. Give it one or more CSS selectors and it prints the text (or an attribute such as `href`) of every match, as plain text, JSON or CSV. When you point it at a live URL it reads the site's `robots.txt` first and politely refuses to fetch pages the site has asked bots to stay away from.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python web_scraper.py SOURCE -s "[NAME=]CSS" [-s ...] [--attr href] [--format text|json|csv]
                      [--limit N] [--base URL] [--robots-file robots.txt]
```
`SOURCE` is a URL or a saved `.html` file. Selectors support tags, `.class`, `#id`, `[attr]`, `[attr=value]` (also `^=`, `$=`, `*=`), the descendant and `>` combinators, and comma lists. Give a selector a name with `price=li b` and the CSV gets a column for it. The exit code is 2 when `robots.txt` disallows the page and 1 when nothing matched.
sections.Example:
```bash
python web_scraper.py page.html -s "link=a" -s "internal=nav a" --attr href --base https://example.com/
```
```
[link] https://example.com/products
[link] https://example.com/about.html
[link] https://example.com/docs
[link] https://example.com/#top
[link] mailto:hello@example.com
[link] https://example.com/docs
[link] https://partner.test/page
[link] javascript:void(0)
[internal] https://example.com/products
[internal] https://example.com/about.html
[internal] https://example.com/docs
[internal] https://example.com/#top
```
sections.Notes:
- Only one page is fetched per run, with an honest `User-Agent`. Scraping is polite, not stealthy: if a site forbids it, the tool stops.
- Selectors with spaces inside attribute values (`[title="a b"]`) are not supported.
- Pages that build their content with JavaScript aren't rendered; you only get the HTML the server sends.
- On the website demo only saved files can be scraped; fetching URLs works on your own computer.

tools.name: price-tracker
tools.summary: Read a product price from a page, keep a history in a CSV and flag price drops.

schema.description: Track a product price over time.

arguments.help: a product page URL, or a saved .html file
CSV file that keeps the price history
compare only, don't add a row
tell me when the price is at or below this
pattern with one group that captures the price

sections.Purpose: Know when something gets cheaper. It reads the price of a product page, compares it with the readings you saved before, and tells you whether it dropped, rose or stayed the same, and whether it's the lowest price yet. Every run can add a row to a CSV, so a daily schedule builds a price history you can chart.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python price_tracker.py SOURCE [--history prices.csv] [--no-record] [--target 50] [--regex PATTERN]
```
`SOURCE` is a product URL or a saved `.html` file. The price is looked up in the page's structured data first, then meta tags and `itemprop="price"`, then your `--regex` (one capture group), and finally the first price with a currency symbol. Without `--history` it just prints the price.
sections.Example:
```bash
python price_tracker.py product.html --history prices.csv --no-record --target 80
```
```
Price now: 79.99 USD
PRICE DROP: 10.00 less than 89.99 on 2026-10-15 (11.1%)
Lowest price seen so far!
At or below your target of 80.00.
(read from structured data)
```
sections.Notes:
- The history CSV has the columns `timestamp, url, price, currency`; each page is tracked by the exact source you gave.
- `--no-record` compares without adding a row, handy for trying a new page.
- Run it from cron or Task Scheduler for a real tracker. Pick a sensible interval, such as once a day.
- Shops that load prices with JavaScript may not show one in the raw HTML; use `--regex` or a saved copy of the rendered page.
- On the website demo only saved files can be read; fetching a URL works on your own computer.

tools.name: html-table-extractor
tools.summary: Export the tables on a web page (or saved .html file) to CSV files. Dry run by default.

arguments.help: a page URL, or a saved .html file
only this table (1 = first); repeat for several

sections.Purpose: Turn the tables on a web page into spreadsheets. tools.name: page-change-detector
tools.summary: Check whether a page's visible content has changed since the last time you looked.

schema.description: Detect when a page's content changes.

arguments.help: a page URL, or a saved .html file
JSON file that remembers the last version
compare with this earlier saved page instead
regex for text to ignore, e.g. dates or visitor counts

sections.Purpose: Find out when a web page changes without staring at it. The tool reduces a page to its visible text, remembers the last version, and tells you which lines were added or removed the next time you run it. The exit code is 1 when something changed, so it slots straight into cron, Task Scheduler or a shell `if`.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python page_change_detector.py SOURCE --state last-seen.json [--ignore REGEX] [--no-update]
python page_change_detector.py SOURCE --previous old-copy.html
```
With `--state` the first run saves a baseline and later runs compare against it, then store the new version. `--no-update` keeps the old baseline so you're told about the change every time until you accept it. `--previous` compares with a saved page and writes nothing. Use `--ignore` for text that always changes, such as `Visitors: \d+`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python page_change_detector.py jobs.html --previous jobs-old.html
```
```
CHANGED: 2 line(s) added, 1 removed.
  - Summer Intern - London
  + Product Designer - Berlin
  + Data Analyst - London
```
sections.Notes:
- Only visible text is compared. Changes to scripts, styles and markup don't count.
- Exit codes: 0 means no change (or a new baseline), 1 means the page changed or couldn't be checked.
- Be kind to the sites you watch: check every few hours, not every few seconds.
- On the website demo only saved files can be compared; watching a URL works on your own computer.

sections.Usage:
```bash
python meta_tag_auditor.py SOURCE [SOURCE ...] [--problems-only] [--strict]
```
Each `SOURCE` is a URL or a saved `.html` file. A missing title or description counts as a failure and makes the exit code 1; other issues are warnings (exit 0) unless you add `--strict`. Use `--problems-only` for a short to-do list.

```bash
python meta_tag_auditor.py seo-page.html --problems-only
```

seo-page.html: 1/12 checks passed
  [WARN] title: only 4 characters (aim for 30-60)
  [FAIL] meta description: missing
  [WARN] canonical link: missing
  [WARN] viewport: missing (not mobile friendly)
  [WARN] html lang: missing
  [WARN] h1: found 2, expected exactly one
  [WARN] robots: page tells search engines not to index it
  [WARN] og:description: missing
  [WARN] og:image: missing
  [WARN] og:url: missing
  [WARN] twitter:card: missing
```

```
Lines starting with `#` in the `--file` are ignored. The exit code is 1 if any address is bad or can't be checked. MX lookups use Cloudflare's public DNS-over-HTTPS service (`cloudflare-dns.com`), so only the domain part of each address is sent, once per domain.
sections.Example:
```bash
python email_validator.py --file emails.txt --no-mx
```
```
ok    alice@acme.test  (syntax only)
ok    bob.smith+news@example.com  (syntax only)
BAD   not-an-email  (missing @)
BAD   sam@@example.org  (needs exactly one @)
BAD   .dot@example.com  (dots in the wrong place in the name part)
ok    name@sub-domain.example.co.uk  (syntax only)
BAD   user@-bad-.com  (domain has invalid characters, hyphens or lengths)
BAD   trailing.dot.@example.com  (dots in the wrong place in the name part)
BAD   ünïcode@example.com  (non-ASCII characters in the name part)
3 of 9 address(es) look fine.
```
sections.Notes:
- A valid-looking address with a mail server can still be a mailbox that doesn't exist. Only sending a message proves that.
- Addresses with non-ASCII characters before the `@` are reported as BAD because many mail systems can't deliver to them.
- A domain with no MX record but an address record is marked `warn`, since mail servers will still try delivering there.
- A "null MX" record (a domain saying it never receives mail) counts as BAD.
- The website demo checks syntax only (`--no-mx`); MX lookups work on your own computer.

tools.name: header-analyzer
tools.summary: Trace the route an email took, and check its SPF, DKIM and DMARC results, from its headers.

schema.description: Trace the hops in an email's headers.

arguments.help: an .eml file, or a text file of headers

sections.Purpose: See where an email really came from. The tool reads a saved message (an `.eml` file, or just its headers pasted into a text file) and lays out the route it took, one hop per `Received` line from the sender's server to yours, with the time each hop took. It also reports the SPF, DKIM and DMARC verdicts your mail provider recorded and flags things that deserve a second look.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python header_analyzer.py message.eml
```
In most mail apps you can save the original message with "Download message", "Show original" or "View source". Warnings cover failed SPF/DKIM/DMARC checks, a Return-Path or Reply-To on a different domain from the sender, missing authentication results, and slow or out-of-order hops. The exit code is 1 when there is at least one warning.
sections.Example:
```bash
python header_analyzer.py message.eml
```
```
From:       Daily Brief <news@brief.example>
To:         Sam Reader <sam@example.org>
Subject:    Your Monday brief
Date:       Mon, 02 Nov 2026 07:29:00 +0000
Message-ID: <brief-1102@brief.example>

Route (3 hop(s), oldest first):
  1. app01.brief.example -> relay.brief.example   2026-11-02 07:29:02 +0000
  2. relay.brief.example -> mx1.example.org   2026-11-02 07:30:05 +0000  (+63s)
  3. mx1.example.org -> inbox.example.org   2026-11-02 07:30:09 +0000  (+4s)
  total transit: 67 seconds

Authentication:
  SPF   pass
  DKIM  pass
  DMARC fail
  signed by brief.example

Warnings:
  ! DMARC result is 'fail'
```
sections.Notes:
- Everything is read from the file; nothing is sent over the network.
- Headers can be forged by the original sender. Only the topmost `Received` lines, added by servers you trust, are reliable.
- Newsletters often send from a sub-domain (such as `mailer.brand.example`); that counts as aligned and isn't flagged.
- If your provider doesn't record `Authentication-Results`, the tool falls back to the `Received-SPF` header.

tools.name: stale-branch-cleaner
tools.summary: Find merged branches nobody has touched for a while, and delete them only with --apply.

schema.description: Find and optionally delete stale merged branches.

arguments.help: branch the others must be merged into
saved for-each-ref output instead of git
saved list of merged branch names
treat this date as today, YYYY-MM-DD (for testing)

sections.Purpose: Tidy up branches that are finished. The tool lists branches that are already merged into your main branch and haven't had a commit for a while (90 days by default), oldest first. Nothing is deleted unless you add `--apply`, and even then only those branches are removed. Unmerged work, the base branch, protected names (`main`, `master`, `develop`, `dev`, `trunk`) and the branch you're on are always left alone.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+, and `git` on your PATH for real repositories.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python stale_branch_cleaner.py [--repo PATH] [--base main] [--days 90] [--apply]
python stale_branch_cleaner.py --remote [--apply]
python stale_branch_cleaner.py --refs branches.txt --merged merged.txt
```
Local branches are deleted with `git branch -d`, which refuses to remove anything unmerged. With `--remote` it works on `origin`'s branches and `--apply` runs `git push origin --delete` for each one, so run the dry run first and read the list. `--refs` and `--merged` read saved output instead of git (dry run only); create them with:
```bash
git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short)%1f%(committerdate:short)%1f%(authorname)%1f%(subject)' refs/heads > branches.txt
git branch --merged main > merged.txt
```
sections.Example:
```bash
python stale_branch_cleaner.py --refs branches.txt --merged merged.txt --today 2026-01-13
```
```
1 stale merged local branch(es) (merged into main, idle 90+ days) out of 5:
  old/experiment                225 days  Max Weber

Dry run - nothing deleted. Add --apply to delete the branches listed above.
```
sections.Notes:
- "Merged" is judged by git from the branch history, so squash-merged branches may not be recognised.
- A deleted local branch can be restored from `git reflog` for a while; a deleted remote branch is harder to bring back.
- Add a `--base` other than `main` if your default branch has a different name.

```bash
python label_auditor.py owner/repo-one owner/repo-two [owner/repo-three ...]
python label_auditor.py --from-file saved-labels.json
```
The exit code is 1 when any difference is found and 0 when the labels all match. Public repositories need no login (60 requests an hour is plenty here); for private ones set `GITHUB_TOKEN` (`export GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_...`, or `$env:GITHUB_TOKEN = "ghp_..."` in PowerShell). It is only sent to the GitHub API and never printed. The tool only reads labels; it never changes them. `--from-file` takes a JSON object mapping each repository to the list of labels GitHub returns.
sections.Example:
```bash
python label_auditor.py --from-file gh-labels.json
```

  'docs': missing in octo-demo/web-app
  'documentation': missing in octo-demo/api-server, octo-demo/data-tools
  'good first issue': missing in octo-demo/web-app, octo-demo/data-tools
